findings.title: order() mixin maps 0-based `order` onto 1-based legacy ordinal-group
findings.body: The new `order($val)` mixin emits the same number for `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` as for the standard `order` property. These are not equivalent: in the 2009 box spec `box-ordinal-group` is 1-based (initial value 1) while `order` is 0-based (initial value 0). Consequences: (a) `@include order(0)` emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 0`, which is invalid and is dropped, and (b) any element given `order(1)` intending it to be placed *after* non-ordered siblings will instead be grouped with them in legacy-box engines, because unordered siblings default to ordinal-group 1. The legacy lines should use `$val + 1` (and the mixin should guard against `$val < 0`). This matters for the new usages `@include order(2)` on `.extra-info-wrapper` and `@include order(3)` on `.d-header .panel`, which only accidentally line up today because `.title` has no explicit order.

findings.title: align-items() forwards modern keywords to legacy properties that do not accept them
findings.body: `align-items($alignment)` passes `$alignment` verbatim to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those legacy properties only accept `start | end | center | baseline | stretch`, so the very common modern values `flex-start` and `flex-end` will produce invalid declarations that are silently dropped, leaving legacy engines (which are precisely the ones receiving `display: -webkit-box` / `-ms-flexbox` from the new `flexbox()` mixin) with the default `stretch` alignment. The current call sites only use `center` and `baseline`, so the bug is latent, but as a shared mixin it will break the first time someone writes `@include align-items(flex-start)`. The mixin should translate `flex-start`/`flex-end` to `start`/`end` for the legacy properties.

findings.title: align-items() has no -moz-box-align although flexbox() emits display: -moz-box
findings.body: `flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` emit `display: -moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box` for old Gecko, and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, but `align-items()` omits `-moz-box-align`. Old Firefox versions therefore get legacy box layout with no cross-axis alignment at all (default stretch), which is exactly the case the prefix fallback was added for: e.g. `.d-header .contents` and `.small-action` will render with stretched, non-centered children instead of the intended vertical centering. Either add `-moz-box-align` or drop the `-moz-box` display fallbacks so the prefix coverage is internally consistent.

findings.title: Making .small-action a flex container breaks right alignment of its button
findings.body: `.small-action` is now `display: flex`, which makes `float` on its direct children a no-op. The `button { float: right; }` rule at the end of the block (and `.topic-avatar { float: left; }`) therefore no longer have any effect: the small-action button will be laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of being pushed to the right edge of the post, because `.small-action-desc` has no `flex: 1`/`flex-grow` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`. The existing `clear: both` on the flex container is likewise dead. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button (or `flex: 1` to `.small-action-desc`) and remove the now-meaningless float/clear declarations.

findings.title: Header .panel right alignment relies on auto margins, which the legacy box fallback does not support
findings.body: `.panel` previously used `float: right`; it now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the flex `.contents`. Auto margins do not distribute free space in the 2009 flexbox (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) that the new `flexbox()` mixin emits as a fallback, and there is no `-webkit-box-pack: end` equivalent. In engines that pick the legacy box display (old WebKit/Gecko builds) the panel with the search/user/hamburger icons will sit flush against the title instead of at the right edge of the header, i.e. a visible header regression for those browsers. Either add the legacy packing properties or drop the legacy `display` fallbacks so those browsers keep the float-based layout.
